title: Tool calling + JSON mode: structured output performance deep-dive

Can KV cache be used across tool-calling flows with long context?
Impact of 4-bit vs 8-bit quantization on structured output accuracy?
What network hops add when on VPC/private deployment?

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-14 16:00 UTC
Duration: 60 minutes
Attendees: Marcus Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Omar Ruiz (Infra Eng), Denise Park (Prod) — Aisha Khan (Veridian Head of ML), Ben Torres (Platform), Rina Patel (Security), Chris Gomez (SRE)

Summary: short technical deep dive on tool-calling + json mode performance, focused on constrained decoding overhead and runtime implications for VPC/on-prem deployments.

00:00 Marcus: hey everyone thanks for joining, we'll jump right in. goal is to show where overhead shows up for strict json or structured outputs when using tool or function calling, and what levers we have at the runtime level
00:18 Aisha: yeah appreciate it, for us the big thing is p99 latency for patient-facing flows — if json validation takes extra seconds it's not acceptable
00:30 Priya: absolutely. quick agenda: 1) decode path overhead in JSON mode, 2) KV cache interactions with tool calls, 3) batching and quantization effects, 4) on-prem/VPC network considerations, and then next steps
00:52 Ben: quick context — we're currently on a mix of hosted endpoints and our private cluster; but for PHI reasons we want everything inside our VPC if possible and need to understand the perf delta
01:10 Marcus: perfect. Priya, you want to kick with the constrained decoding analysis?
01:15 Priya: sure. so, when we force a model into constrained decoding to emit strict JSON, two main things happen: decoding runtime does extra token-level checks (schema/token filters) and we sometimes run rejection sampling or constrained beam search to enforce structure. that adds CPU/GPU decision hops and can increase per-token latency, especially on small-batch low-latency configs
01:43 Priya: typical overhead ranges we see are around +5-25% latency on generation depending on how strict the constraints are and if you hit many invalid tokens early in the sequence
02:02 Chris: is that because the runtime is doing retry loops or because the model is slower?
02:10 Priya: both. RTT for the sampler, plus additional kernel invocations if we need to re-evaluate logits after masking. also if you use a post-hoc parser with retries that's extra round trips. we prefer in-run constrained decoding where the runtime applies token masks natively
02:35 Rina: what about JSON mode's impact on correctness when we quantize to 4-bit? we worry about malformed output for downstream parsers
02:45 Priya: good question. quantization affects probability estimates; with extreme quant (4-bit) you can see higher entropy and token distribution shifts which makes strict constraints more likely to trigger retries. in our internal tests, 8-bit qint8 maintains structured output fidelity in ~95% of cases, 4-bit needs validation and sometimes a small model finetune or calibration set to maintain schema conformance
03:15 Marcus: that matches what we've seen — quantization saves cost but you pay in output reliability for constrained schemas unless you run a small eval+calibration step
03:28 Aisha: any numbers you can share on p95/p99 with and without constraints?
03:33 Priya: rough numbers from a recent internal benchmark on a 2048-context model: unconstrained p50 60ms, p95 220ms, p99 420ms. with strict JSON constraints using in-run masking and no retries p50 70ms, p95 260ms, p99 520ms. if you include retry loops the p99 can blow up to >1s depending on retry budget
03:58 Ben: ok that p99 bump is concerning. can batching help here or will batching make it worse for latency?
04:05 Priya: batching helps throughput but will increase per-request latency for single-shot low-latency flows. our recommendation: for patient-facing UI keep batch size minimal and tune timeout windows. for backend pipelines you can batch aggressively. also KV cache can reduce token generation if you have repeated prefixes
04:30 Omar: can you explain KV cache behavior with tool calls? our flows do a lot of tool invocation: model emits a call to a tool (e.g., lookup), then continues generation. does KV cache persist across the hop?
04:45 Priya: good point; tool calling flows often flush or rehydrate KV state depending on routing. in our runtime we keep KV cache live across synchronous tool calls if the tool is executed inline and the model continues within the same session. if there's a remote tool that induces a network round trip we may need to snapshot and rehydrate which adds latency
05:10 Chris: so inline vs async tool execution matters for the runtime latency profile
05:14 Priya: exactly. inline synchronous tool calls — lower overhead if co-located and KV kept warm. remote tool calls or multi-service orchestration require snapshot/rehydrate and you'll see additional latency and possible KV mismatch complexity
05:32 Rina: and in VPC/on-prem that snapshotting may cross subnets, is that measurable?
05:38 Omar: yes, if tool runs in a different availability zone or on-prem system the network hop is significant. we recommend colocating runtime + critical tool containers within the same VPC subnet when low-latency is needed
05:55 Marcus: another lever is bounded decoding length with early stopping heuristics to reduce wasted tokens when constraints are violated — that helps p99
06:10 Priya: also prefix caching: if many calls share the same starting instructions you can cache KV states for those prefixes and serve subsequent requests from warm state, which lowers token compute drastically
06:30 Ben: curious about quantization + constrained decoding combined — you said 8-bit is usually ok, any mode recommendations?
06:36 Priya: yes, 8-bit or dynamic quant with calibration is the safe starting point. for JSON mode, we often recommend enabling a "soft constraints" pass first — run with masked logits but allow a single corrective postprocess if needed — that keeps latency bounded while preserving high schema conformance
06:58 Denise: what about model selection? smaller models with stronger decoding controls vs larger models — tradeoffs?
07:05 Priya: larger models are more forgiving with constraints; they tend to hit valid tokens more quickly so fewer retries. but they cost more. smaller distilled models may need more constrained search and thus more retries. so pick a model with enough capacity for schema complexity or use a two-step pipeline: larger model to produce structured output then distilled model for cheaper generation where appropriate
07:36 Aisha: for our use case we need high correctness on JSON schema but limited budget — sounds like maybe run the heavy-lift model for critical steps and cache results / reuse them
07:46 Marcus: yes, caching outputs, prefix caching, and deterministic reruns for critical calls is a common pattern
07:55 Priya: moving on to batching: if you batch at the runtime layer, you get better GPU utilization and lower cost per token, but you must balance latency SLOs. we offer continuous batching and adaptive timeouts to minimize latency impact for mixed workloads
08:15 Ben: can the runtime prioritize low-latency requests and still batch them?
08:20 Omar: we have priority routing — low-latency requests can get dedicated slots or run on smaller batch windows; also Dedicated pools let you reserve capacity for low-latency workloads
08:35 Rina: SSO/audit question: if we run in our VPC, do audit logs capture token-level logs or only metadata?
08:43 Marcus: by default Redwood captures request/response metadata and offers configurable PII redaction. for Private deployments we integrate with customer KMS and you can push audit logs to your SIEM — token-level logs can be captured but it's opt-in and we recommend redaction
09:05 Chris: network topology: how many extra hops if we go Private vs Hosted?
09:12 Omar: depends on placement. Hosted means a public edge and our internal network; VPC private deployment will remove public edges but add internal hops to customer tool services. typical extra latency is 5-20ms for intra-region VPC egress, but worst-case cross-AZ or on-prem connections add 50-200ms depending on routing and firewall inspection
09:35 Aisha: ok that 200ms worst-case is big for p99. we need an end-to-end bench in our VPC to know for sure
09:43 Priya: we'll run exactly that. we'll instrument p50/p95/p99 and breakdown: model compute, tokenization, KV snapshot/rehydrate, network, and tool execution time.
10:00 Ben: more on measurement: can you run the benchmark with both quant profiles and with/without constrained decoding so we can see tradeoffs?
10:08 Priya: yes that's part of the plan — baseline (unconstrained), constrained-inrun, constrained-with-retries, and then quant profiles 16-bit, 8-bit, 4-bit with calibration. we'll produce a spreadsheet with per-condition p50/p95/p99 and cost estimates
10:27 Rina: security — for VPC pilot what infra access do you need? we prefer minimal access and a runner approach where Redwood ships a container that we run inside our VPC
10:36 Marcus: we support that; Private deployment can be customer-run with our control-plane integration. Omar, we should note the runner image and required ports in the follow-up
10:44 Omar: noted. we'll document required ports, egress rules, and recommended placement (same subnet as tool services)
10:52 Aisha: any gotchas around tokenization or tokenizer mismatch in quantized models or on different runtimes?
10:58 Priya: tokenizer consistency is critical; we ship tokenizer bundles with models. if you run on different runtime versions ensure tokenizers match. mismatched tokenization can cause off-by-one tokens and break structured output constraints
11:15 Ben: what's the overhead of streaming structured output vs one-shot generation?
11:21 Priya: streaming allows progressive validation and earlier tool calls, which is good for perceived latency. the challenge is enforcing global JSON validity: when streaming you need either an outer wrapper approach or incremental schema enforcement. streaming increases complexity but can reduce time-to-first-byte dramatically
11:40 Chris: for patient flows we'd probably prefer streaming for responsiveness but we also need full-JSON correctness before acting
11:48 Priya: pattern: stream the tentative output for UI while simultaneously running a quick validation pass server-side and only trigger downstream actions after validation success
12:05 Marcus: any final questions?
12:10 Aisha: one more — can we preserve KV cache across deployments if we switch from hosted to private?
12:16 Priya: yes, KV snapshots are portable at serialization level but you need compatible model versions and tokenizer versions. it's doable but we advise a migration plan and validation to ensure cached entries still map correctly
12:32 Ben: good. that covers most of it. let's recap next steps
12:40 Marcus: recap: Veridian will share 10 canonical prompts and schemas by 2025-10-20; Priya will run the constrained-decoding + quant benchmarks and deliver spreadsheet by 2025-10-22; Omar will provide VPC topology and runner requirements by 2025-10-18; Redwood to schedule pilot in customer's VPC for week of 2025-10-27.
12:58 Rina: thanks everyone, appreciate the level of detail
13:03 Marcus: thanks all, we'll follow up with the benchmark plan and a calendar invite for the pilot prep
13:10 (meeting ends)

Notes about transcript quality: medium — occasional mis-heard terms (e.g., "K V cache" vs "KV cache"), some punctuation dropped, typical Fireflies-style export.
